title: Bring a recommendation, not just a problem
body: "Here are three options and I'd pick B, here's why" gets a faster yes and builds more trust than "what should we do?"

title: Great simplifiers
body: Great leaders are almost always great simplifiers.
author: Colin Powell

title: Disagreeing with your manager in the room
body: Your manager makes a decision in front of the team that you think is wrong. What is the best move?

options.label: Push back immediately, in the room
Support it in the room, then raise your disagreement privately afterward
Go around them to their manager

explanation: Undermining a decision publicly damages trust on both sides even when you turn out to be right. Raise it privately, and quickly.

title: Alignment that quietly eroded
body: A skip-level conversation revealed that a peer team had been deprioritized by the same exec sponsor everyone assumed was fully bought in — an alignment nobody had rechecked in six months. Alignment decays; it has to be re-verified, not assumed.

title: Check a priority you're guessing at
body: Identify one stakeholder whose priorities you're assuming rather than actually know. Schedule 20 minutes with them this week.

title: Translate your work into their metrics
body: An executive sponsor does not need your architecture diagram — they need to know how this moves the number they are accountable for.

title: Over-communicate risk, under-commit on dates
body: Flag a risk before it's confirmed so there are no surprises later. Don't promise a date you're not sure of just to sound confident in the room.

title: Silence is not buy-in
body: A manager assumed an exec sponsor was fully aligned because they raised no objections in the kickoff — and got blindsided by pushback at the quarterly review. Absence of pushback in a meeting is not confirmation; ask for it explicitly.

title: Ask how they prefer to receive bad news
body: Some managers want it immediately and raw; others want a beat to process, with a proposed next step attached. Guessing wrong costs trust either way.

title: Give the one-line answer before the context
body: A busy executive sponsor wants the bottom line first and the reasoning only if they ask for it. Leading with background reads as stalling.

title: Hearing it from the skip-level first
body: A manager learned from a skip-level that their own manager had been quietly fielding complaints about the team for months — nobody wanted to be the one to say it directly. Ask often what's being said about your team when you're not in the room.

title: Ask what would make their job easier
body: Ask your manager this week: "what's the one thing that would make your job easier right now?" Then go do it.

title: Credit visibly, raise concerns privately
body: The reverse of how most people default — and it is what actually builds trust upward over time.

title: A disagreement with an adjacent team
body: You disagree with a decision an adjacent team's lead made that affects your roadmap. What's the best first move?

options.label: Go directly to that lead first, assuming good intent, before looping in anyone above either of you
Work around the decision without saying anything
Raise it in a large cross-team meeting

explanation: Escalating before attempting a direct conversation reads as going over someone's head — and the disagreement is often resolvable with context neither side had yet.

title: Show your work when you ask for resources
body: "I need two more engineers" lands far weaker than "here's what we can and can't deliver at current headcount, and here's the tradeoff at plus two."
